# What the Dark Was For

In January of 1994, an earthquake struck Northridge, California, in the hours before dawn. The shaking knocked out power across Los Angeles, and in the blacked-out city, people who stumbled outside reported something strange. Callers rang emergency lines and local observatories, not only about broken gas mains and buckled freeways, but about the sky itself. They described a vast, luminous, silvery cloud hanging over the mountains — enormous, radiant, unfamiliar. Some worried it was a sign of further catastrophe. What they were seeing, for the first time in many of their lives, was the Milky Way.

The story has been told so often in discussions of light pollution that it risks becoming folklore, but it is folklore of the truest kind: it names a real condition. A single night of darkness returned to a modern city a spectacle that every human being who ever lived before the twentieth century knew intimately. The earthquake did not put a new thing in the sky. It removed the one thing we had put in the way of the oldest thing of all.

I want to make an argument here that is difficult to state without sounding either nostalgic or alarmist, and I will try to do neither. It is simply this: night, as our ancestors knew it, is extinct, and we have barely begun to inventory what went extinct with it. For nearly the entire human story, darkness was not the dimming of the world but its other half — arguably the larger half, since for most people in most centuries, life was conducted by daylight and then surrendered to a night of twelve, thirteen, fourteen hours, especially in winter. That night was not a paler version of day. It was a different country, with its own borders, its own inhabitants, its own laws, its own sleep, its own god. We colonized it in the space of about four generations, and we now live in a world with no true night anywhere, only a planetary twilight that never fully ends.

Consider how absolute the old dark was. There was no glow on the horizon from a distant city, because there were no distant cities of light. A moonless night was a blackness most of us have never experienced and cannot experience indoors, where even switched-off rooms swim in the orange bleed of streetlights through curtains. Scholars who reconstruct preindustrial nights emphasize that darkness then was not an inconvenience; it was an environment. You did not have a dark night in your life the way you have a rainy day. You had it the way a fish has water.

And into that darkness, human beings carried the most interesting thing about us: our ability to sleep in shifts.

The historian Roger Ekirch, combing diaries, court records, medical texts, and household papers from centuries of European life, found hundreds of references to something modern sleep science had assumed was impossible: people did not sleep through the night. They slept in two segments. There was the "first sleep," which began an hour or two after dusk and lasted perhaps four hours. Then people woke — naturally, unpanicked, even cheerfully — into an interval they sometimes called "the watch." During the watch, in a darkness broken only by embers, they prayed, and they often timed the interval by reciting a fixed number of psalms, like monks of their own private order. They talked. They tended the fire. They smoked, they visited neighbors by moonlight, they reflected on dreams, which were understood to arrive during the first sleep and to matter. A sixteenth-century French physician advised couples that the best time to conceive was after the first sleep, when body and spirit were rested but not yet weary. Then came the second sleep, which ran until dawn, or until the rooster, or until the bell.

This was not a regional quirk. The same pattern shows up in French *premier sommeil*, in Italian *primo sonno*, in accounts from Africa, South Asia, and South America. It appears to be what human sleep does when human beings are given enough darkness. In the 1990s, the researcher Thomas Wehr tested the proposition in a laboratory, giving volunteers a month of fourteen-hour nights — an approximation of a winter darkness no modern schedule allows. After a few weeks of adjustment, their sleep split cleanly in two: a long stretch, then an hour or two of quiet, contented wakefulness with a distinctive hormonal signature, then another long stretch. Given darkness, the old pattern re-emerged like a seed sprouting in a drawer.

Which raises an uncomfortable possibility: the unbroken eight hours we treat as biological law is largely an industrial artifact, and our epidemic of 2 a.m. wakefulness — the ceiling-staring, the glowing phone, the dread that something is wrong with us — may be, in part, an artifact of lost dark. Our ancestors woke in the middle of the night all the time. They just didn't have anything to be anxious about, because waking at two was not a malfunction. It was the watch, a room of its own, a hidden hour that has been demolished by the light left on in the hall.

The old night had a character, and the character was not gentle. Night was when the poor rationed their light — a tallow candle smoked and stank and gave off a weak sputter; beeswax was for churches and the rich; the very poor burned rushlights, peeled reeds dipped in grease that flared for a few minutes each. The very word *curfew* preserves the old night's discipline: from the French *couvre-feu*, the bell that ordered fires banked and everyone indoors. Night was when fear had jurisdiction. The word *nightmare* carries a fossil inside it — the *mare*, a demon believed to sit on the sleeper's chest, a figure that appears in one guise or another in folklore across the world, because the experience it describes, sleep paralysis, happens to everyone everywhere in the dark. Witches flew at night. Ghosts walked at night. The dead, the damned, the desperate, and the dreaming all kept night hours.

But fear was only half the ledger. Night was also where the constrained self went to breathe. Daylight belonged to masters, employers, husbands, schedules; night, opaque and unpoliced, was a cloak. Lovers kept it. Servants kept it. Thieves and runaway apprentices kept it. Bakers rose into it, midwives moved through it, and the watchman's cry threaded through it like a slow heartbeat. Night had its own population, its own economy, its own etiquette. It was, in the fullest sense, a country.

And over that country hung its sun. It is almost impossible now to convey what the moon was, because we have demoted it. To us the full moon is an ornament we notice while driving. To our ancestors it was infrastructure. The word *month* is the word *moon*; the first calendars were moons; planting, fishing, travel, and celebration were scheduled by its phases. The harvest moon was an actual technology — the full moon nearest the autumn equinox rises soon after sunset for several evenings running, and it gave farmers real, working evenings of light to bring the crop in. An old proverb called the moon the lamp of the poor, and it was exactly that: the one light free to everyone, level with the ground, impartial. Poets across cultures built a vocabulary around it that we now read as pure fancy but was once simple description. Li Bai, drinking alone, raises his cup to invite the moon to join him — because at night, outdoors, under a light that traveled ninety-three million fewer miles than the sun's, the moon felt present in a way we have forgotten light can feel. In Japan, *tsukimi*, moon-viewing, is still practiced with autumn grasses and small white dumplings shaped like clouds — a liturgy of looking at light.

Then we built our own. The conquest of the night proceeded by fuels, and each fuel was an empire. Whale oil came first in America's account — the hunt for spermaceti, which burned brighter and cleaner than tallow, sent ships to the ends of the ocean after creatures that had their own songs and their own dark, so that people in Nantucket parlors could read an extra hour. Petroleum's first great market was not cars but kerosene lamps. Then came gas mains threading under London in the early 1800s, street by street, and then, in 1882, Edison's Pearl Street Station switched on, and the grid began its patient work of making light effectively free. And when something becomes free, we spend it extravagantly. Today light pours out of parking lots, empty office towers at 3 a.m., billboards, greenhouses, and the fringes of highways, billions of fixtures burning because they can. From orbit, the earth at night is a map of us — and the map is drawn in the one ink that erases everything else.

The ledger of costs is long, and the first line is the sky itself. The most comprehensive atlas of artificial night-sky brightness, assembled in 2016, found that more than eighty percent of humanity lives under light-polluted skies. More than a third of all people — sixty percent of Europeans, nearly eighty percent of North Americans — cannot see the Milky Way from where they live. A child raised in a bright city may grow to adulthood having seen a few dozen stars, when the human inheritance is thousands, organized into patterns that every culture on earth independently named.

Because the sky was not decoration. It was the first text. The constellations were humanity's first stories, told and retold around fires for purposes of memory and meaning before writing existed. They were also the first calendar: the heliacal rising of Sirius announced the Nile's flood and anchored Egypt's year; the Pleiades marked planting and harvest on continents that had never heard of each other. Polaris was the first compass. It is not sentimental to suggest that religion, philosophy, mathematics, and the very sense of the infinite owe their origins to people lying under an unobstructed sky and failing, magnificently, to find its edge. Everyone who ever lived before roughly 1900 saw that sky on clear nights. Everyone born after 1950 mostly hasn't. It is hard to think of another shared human experience of that duration which has ended so quietly, and without a treaty.

The second line of the ledger is written by everything else that is alive. Darkness is not an absence; it is habitat, and we are destroying it. Sea turtle hatchlings, which navigate toward the brighter seaward horizon, crawl instead toward the sodium glow of beach towns and die in parking lots. Migrating birds, which navigate by stars and moonlight, are drawn into the beams of city skylines — when researchers studied New York's September 11 tribute lights, they found the beams altered the behavior of over a million birds in the seven nights examined, and that simply dimming the lights halfway let most of them go. We used to say moths fly into flames because they mistake lamps for the moon; newer research suggests something sadder, that the light simply blinds them, swamping the faint celestial signals their eyes were built for. Fireflies court with light, and cannot be heard over ours. The largest animal migration on earth happens every single night, when trillions of plankton rise toward the surface in the dark — and coastal skyglow measurably flattens that great breath of the ocean. Even coral, spawning in synchronized moonlit events, keeps a calendar we are washing out.

And our own bodies keep it too. The retina contains cells, discovered only around the turn of this century, whose entire job is to report darkness to the brain's clock, and the blue-rich light we now flood ourselves with after sundown suppresses melatonin with a specificity evolution never prepared us for. The World Health Organization has classified night shift work — human labor in permanent light — as probably carcinogenic. The phrase sounds absurd until you remember what shift work abolishes: not just sleep, but night, the substance our physiology is written in.

Perhaps the deepest cost is the one hardest to measure. The dark does work in us. It is when the brain consolidates the day's memory and runs the strange maintenance of dreaming. It is when the wandering, self-reflective networks take over and produce the insights that daylight's focus crowds out. More than that, the old dark was the primary source of awe available to our species — the nightly encounter with scale, with distances that do not negotiate. Awe is not a luxury; people who experience it reliably become more generous, humbler, more oriented toward something larger than their own concerns. A civilization that cannot see the stars is a civilization starved of its oldest source of awe, and we should not be surprised at what rushes in to fill the vacancy.

And yet almost none of this is irreversible, which is the strange good news. Blackouts keep proving it: when the Northeast went dark in 2003, there were reports of New Yorkers seeing the band of the Milky Way from Manhattan rooftops, crowds looking up at a sky that had simply been waiting behind the light. Whole regions now certify themselves as dark-sky reserves, replacing shielded, warmer, lower lamps, because the solution to light pollution is not darkness ideology — it is better lighting, aimed down, timed off, spent like the resource it is rather than spilled like sewage. And the personal version is available to anyone with a porch light and a switch. It takes about half an hour of true darkness for the eye's chemistry to rebuild and the stars to come back one magnitude at a time, first the bright anchors, then the faint multitude, until the sky is again the thing it always was. That half hour is a kind of parable: the stars do not leave. They are merely outranked, and they return the moment we dim.

The dark was never the absence of light. It was the presence of everything else — the stars, the moon, the watch between two sleeps, the moths and the spawning coral, the awe, the stories, the deep restorative strangeness of a world half with-held from us every day. It is still there. It costs nothing but the courage to flip a switch and stand, briefly, the way our ancestors stood for two hundred thousand years, looking up into the country we were born for.
